entry.title: The Art of Thinking Small – Europe's M1E Revolution Explored
entry.summary: At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, Citroën’s reborn 2CV offered an intriguing glimpse of what Europe’s small-car market could look like from 2028. Compact, electric, full of character and targeting a price of around €15,000, it represents a return to the idea that affordable cars can still be desirable. Behind that vision…
entry.content:
Citroën didn't stop at the passenger car. Alongside the 2CV, Paris brought the wonderfully boxy 2CV Fourgonnette Concept, a modern interpretation of the little delivery van that once served shopkeepers, farmers and tradespeople across Europe.

It offers an intriguing glimpse of how the affordable electric-car movement could eventually extend into commercial vehicles. A small, lightweight electric van with modest running costs could make enormous sense for local businesses.

There is one important distinction. The proposed M1E classification applies to passenger cars rather than commercial vehicles, and Citroën describes the Fourgonnette as a design study rather than a confirmed production model.

Nevertheless, the principle seems too sensible to overlook. If Europe can rediscover the affordable small car, perhaps the affordable little van could follow.


Our TNY rendering imagines how Citroën’s 2CV concept might evolve into a production-ready car for 2028. The original, unveiled in 1948, remained in production until 1990, with more than five million examples built across the 2CV family. Its appeal came from comfort, simplicity, practicality and a character rarely found in inexpensive cars.

Citroën has made affordable city cars work more recently. Built from 2005 to 2022, the C1 shared its development and Czech production line with the Peugeot 107/108 and Toyota Aygo, spreading costs across three brands. When it disappeared, Citroën was left with a sizeable gap between the Ami quadricycle and the larger C3.

At just 3.76 metres long, the new 2CV could fill that space. Citroën is targeting around €15,000, an ambitious figure when the ë-C3 starts at £18,495 in Britain after a £1,500 government grant, itself great value in the small car market. Making it affordable is one challenge; making it desirable is where the 2CV name could shine.


Few manufacturers understand the appeal of a small car quite like Fiat. The original 500 helped put post-war Italy on wheels, while the Panda of 1980 turned minimalism into something ingenious. The Cinquecento and Seicento carried that tradition into the 1990s, proving that affordable needn't mean forgettable.

Our TNY Koala imagines the next chapter: a friendly, compact electric Fiat taking inspiration from the Panda without simply recreating the past. It would give Fiat a useful step between the Topolino quadricycle and today's 500 and Grande Panda, combining proper small-car versatility with a genuinely compact footprint.

UK pricing makes the possibility especially interesting. The Topolino starts at £8,995, the electric 500e at £17,245 after a £3,750 government grant, and the Grande Panda Hybrid at £19,995.

If the future Koala arrived below £20,000, Fiat could offer four distinct entry-level models under that threshold — an increasingly unusual breadth of affordable small cars.


Our rear three-quarter rendering keeps the Koala's design pleasingly straightforward, with a practical tailgate and simple, distinctive lighting. It is the sort of car that could remain attractive without a complete redesign every few years.

While the styling and Koala name remain speculative, Fiat's forthcoming small EV is expected to share Stellantis's new E-Car architecture with the Citroën 2CV. Production of the first E-Car models is planned for Italy in 2028, allowing development costs to be spread across different brands.

That scale becomes particularly important under the proposed M1E framework. Eligible small electric cars built in the EU could count as 1.3 vehicles towards manufacturers' fleet CO₂ calculations until 2034. The European Commission also hopes to limit new regulatory requirements over a ten-year period.

Neither measure guarantees a low purchase price, and existing safety standards remain, but both could encourage longer production runs, modest facelifts and better-finished affordable cars.


Peugeot has an obvious opportunity within this emerging family of small electric cars. The original 108 disappeared in 2022, leaving the larger 208 as Peugeot's smallest conventional passenger car. Our TNY rendering imagines its return as a 4-metre electric supermini, combining Peugeot's latest design language with the affordable engineering developed for Citroën and Fiat.

But why stop at three brands? Stellantis has already confirmed that its E-Car programme is intended to support multiple manufacturers, spreading development costs across greater production volumes.

Peugeot could offer something sharper and sportier, while Opel and Vauxhall could develop their own interpretations for continental European and British customers. Each could share the same fundamental engineering while retaining a distinct appearance and personality.

Although additional models remain unconfirmed, the potential is considerable. With an expensive new platform already under development, expanding the family across Stellantis could make affordable electric cars considerably more viable.


If the 108 represents the return of the affordable city car, our Peugeot 1008 explores a different opportunity. Roughly four metres long, with an upright crossover stance and the assertive face of Peugeot's latest electric models, this TNY concept sits beneath the 2008 but aims to feel substantial, refined and desirable.

M1E is often discussed as a route to €15,000 EVs. Yet the proposed rules define the category by being fully electric and no longer than 4.2 metres; they set no price ceiling or power limit. What if Peugeot used the same shared Stellantis foundations to build something genuinely upmarket?

Our hypothetical brief imagines around 150hp, a 250-mile WLTP target and a price close to £27,000, with particular attention paid to ride comfort, sound insulation, interior materials and long-term durability. These are TNY ambitions, not confirmed specifications or capabilities of the E-Car platform.

The Commission's proposed ten-year period of regulatory stability could strengthen that business case, letting Peugeot invest in a carefully finished small car and keep it attractive through a long production life, with restrained facelifts and evolving technology. M1E needn't only make small cars cheaper; it could make them better.


Renault Group may have an even clearer opportunity to make M1E work. Its all-new Dacia Spring provides a compelling starting point: now built in Slovenia, measuring 3.85 metres long and priced from €17,900 in France before incentives.

Underneath sits Renault Group's cost-conscious RG-EV Small architecture, developed to deliver modern electric motoring without unnecessary expense.

Our TNY Sandero EV imagines that thinking applied to something more substantial. Taking inspiration from the new Spring's upright stance, protective cladding and crisp lighting, we've developed a five-door hatchback with the passenger space and luggage capacity expected of a Sandero. It would be a genuinely useful everyday car, rather than a purely urban runabout.

At around 4.1 metres, it would remain comfortably within M1E's proposed limit. Today's petrol Sandero starts at £14,765 in Britain, setting an understandably demanding benchmark for any electric successor.


From behind, our Sandero EV retains Dacia's practical priorities: an upright tailgate, robust bumper and useful proportions rather than a fashionable sloping roofline. Yet its greater size is also why it needn't be the cheapest Renault Group electric car.

The Spring and Twingo are compact four-seaters; a five-seat Sandero offering more boot space, potentially a larger battery and greater all-round versatility would naturally occupy a different position.

The real challenge is staying below the Renault 5 E-Tech, which currently starts at £21,495 in Britain after a £1,500 government grant. A Sandero EV needn't undercut the smaller Spring or Twingo to make sense. With shared LFP technology, simplified components and the prospect of M1E regulatory stability, Renault Group could produce a spacious, lower-cost alternative to the Renault 5.

European manufacturing could bring additional proposed CO₂ incentives, too, although neither a production Sandero EV nor its specification or price has been confirmed.


Dacia looks ideally placed to exploit M1E, but Renault itself has considerably less room for another small electric car. The new Twingo E-Tech provides an accessible entry point, with the Renault 5 and 4 already covering the ground above. Add an all-new Clio, arriving in Britain in 2027 with petrol and hybrid powertrains, and Renault's smaller-car range looks unusually complete, modern and competitively priced.

Even the refreshed Mégane E-Tech almost straddles the M1E boundary. At 4,199mm long, it sits just 1mm below the proposed 4.2-metre limit.

Its latest version starts at £28,245 in Britain after the £3,750 government Electric Car Grant, bringing a 67kWh LFP battery, 220hp, up to 306 miles of WLTP range and 165kW rapid charging. That's a remarkably strong package for the money, without needing another model squeezed into the range.

For now, the clearest Renault Group opportunity to broaden affordable electric motoring may therefore sit with Dacia.


Volkswagen revealed the ID.EVERY1 concept in March 2025, previewing a 3.88-metre electric car scheduled for production in 2027 and targeting around €20,000. Our TNY ID.Lupo rendering imagines how that concept might evolve into a production Volkswagen, reviving one of the brand's familiar small-car names.

Its timing could prove fortunate. M1E remains a proposal, but the intended 4.2-metre ceiling means the ID.EVERY1 is already the right size.

Volkswagen could engineer the car around the expected framework from day one, rather than face significant revisions later. Whether it receives the proposed benefits will depend on the final regulations and where the vehicle is manufactured.

The ID. Polo now starts at £22,445 in Britain after the £1,500 government grant. Yet Volkswagen still needs a smaller electric car capable of bringing its entry price closer to £15,000–£20,000, and the ID.Lupo could be vital to keeping the brand competitive.


Škoda has already demonstrated the value of sharing small-car engineering. Its original Citigo was closely related to the Volkswagen up! and SEAT Mii, while the electric Citigo-e iV arrived in 2019. Our TNY rendering imagines a modern successor, sharing its foundations with Volkswagen's forthcoming entry-level EV.

The Fabia and Scala demonstrate Škoda's ability to deliver generous space and practicality for modest money, while the new Epiq brings that philosophy to electric crossovers. However, with prices starting at £24,950, the Epiq retains a relatively high entry price in an increasingly competitive small-EV market. A smaller, more affordable Citigo EV could therefore fill an important gap, giving this value-conscious brand a genuinely accessible electric city car.

Volkswagen Group already shares development costs across the ID.Polo, ID.Cross, Cupra Raval and Škoda Epiq. Extending that approach to smaller models could make M1E particularly attractive.

From Stellantis to Renault Group and Volkswagen Group, Europe's established manufacturers have the brands, experience and industrial capacity to embrace this opportunity. But affordable electric motoring needn't remain exclusively European territory. Chinese manufacturers willing to establish production within the EU could also benefit, potentially bringing fresh competition to Europe's smallest-car market.


MG could become one of the most interesting beneficiaries of M1E. Its petrol and Hybrid+ MG3, alongside the electric MG4 and newer MG4 EV Urban, have helped establish the Chinese-owned British marque as a serious contender across Europe. Yet there remains an opportunity for something smaller and more affordable.

Our TNY MG GO, previously explored in Design Studio, imagines a practical five-door electric hatchback measuring approximately four metres long. With a target price below £20,000, it could give MG an appealing entry point into electric ownership, complementing its increasingly comprehensive small-car range.

Crucially, MG has announced a €200 million manufacturing facility in Galicia, Spain, with production scheduled for 2028 and capacity for 120,000 vehicles annually.

Under the proposed European rules, Chinese ownership would not necessarily prevent M1E eligibility. However, EU assembly alone would be insufficient: vehicles would also need to satisfy European component or battery-origin requirements.

Whether MG would manufacture such a small car in Spain remains speculative, but the opportunity is certainly there.


Chery is already thinking smaller. In April 2026, its head of engineering, Peter Matkin, confirmed development of a new architecture for cars measuring less than four metres, opening opportunities beyond the group's predominantly SUV-focused range.

TNY recently explored that possibility with our Jaecoo 2 rendering: a distinctive 3.9-metre hatchback, with an estimated £19,000 starting price. An electric version would comfortably satisfy M1E's proposed dimensional requirements, although the model and its specifications remain entirely speculative.

Chery also has a growing European manufacturing presence. Through its partnership with Spanish manufacturer EBRO, the company is expanding production at Nissan's former Barcelona factory. Pre-production Jaecoo 5 models are expected by December 2026, with series production targeted for early 2027.

There is no confirmed plan to manufacture a Jaecoo 2 in Spain. However, a small electric model built there, incorporating sufficient European-sourced components or batteries, could potentially qualify for M1E's proposed incentives.

For Chery, European manufacturing and a new small-car platform could prove an exceptionally useful combination.


Perhaps it is fitting to finish where we began. The original 2CV demonstrated that affordable motoring could be practical, comfortable and full of character. Nearly eight decades after its introduction, those qualities remain just as relevant.

M1E will not transform Europe's small-car market overnight. The regulations remain proposals, batteries are still expensive, and manufacturers must find ways to make European production commercially competitive.

Yet the possibilities are considerable. From a €15,000 Citroën to a more sophisticated Peugeot, an affordable Dacia or even a Chinese-designed car manufactured in Europe, there needn't be one formula for success.

Above all, greater regulatory stability could encourage manufacturers to invest properly in their smallest cars, creating designs worth keeping in production for years rather than constantly replacing them.

If M1E succeeds, its greatest achievement may not simply be making small cars cheaper. It could make them genuinely desirable again.

TNY Design Studio renderings are independent, speculative illustrations and do not represent confirmed manufacturer designs or production plans. All proposed specifications and prices are estimates unless otherwise stated. M1E legislation remains subject to approval and amendment.

entry.title: From Bestseller to Beyond – TNY Design Studio Explores Jaecoo's Future
entry.summary: Few new car brands have arrived in Britain with quite the impact of Jaecoo. Launched here in January 2025, the Chinese SUV marque had already put its Jaecoo 7 at the top of the UK sales chart twice by September 2026, recording 10,813 registrations in that month alone. Behind it stands Chery,…
entry.content:
Jaecoo’s next move could be its smallest SUV yet. Reports suggest the Jaecoo 3 will measure around 4.2 metres long, putting it alongside rivals such as the Ford Puma and Renault 4.

The newcomer is reportedly being developed with European buyers in mind, with hybrid and fully electric versions both possible. A 2027 launch has been suggested, although Jaecoo has yet to confirm a date or release final specifications.

For TNY Design Studio, we’ve imagined how Jaecoo’s familiar styling might translate into a smaller SUV. Our rendering keeps the bold front grille and angular bodywork of the larger models, with compact proportions suited to British roads. It could become an interesting alternative in an increasingly competitive market.


The Jaecoo 5 offers a useful indication of where the smaller Jaecoo 3 might fit. Measuring 4,380mm long, it starts at £24,555 on the road, while the larger Jaecoo 7 measures 4,500mm and costs from £30,165 in petrol form.

Both share the upright, distinctly Range Rover-inspired styling that has helped Jaecoo attract attention in Britain, offering a premium appearance without premium-brand prices. At approximately 4.2 metres long, the forthcoming Jaecoo 3 would be 180mm shorter than the 5.

Based on the existing range, we estimate that an entry-level hybrid could start somewhere around £20,000–£22,000, with an electric version potentially costing more. That would place it among some fiercely competitive small SUVs, while retaining the design that has made its larger siblings so recognisable.


Jaecoo has proved that distinctive styling and competitive pricing can win over British buyers. Yet the small-SUV market is fiercely competitive, with established rivals offering plenty of choice. If the Jaecoo 3 is to follow the success of the 5 and 7, can it deliver enough to stand out?

At the opposite end of Jaecoo’s expanding range, something considerably larger could be on the horizon. The Jaecoo 8 has only recently arrived in Britain, bringing seven-seat practicality and a starting price of £45,500. Yet reports suggest an even more ambitious model is being prepared: the Jaecoo 9, a potential new flagship aimed at the luxury SUV market.

The likely foundation is Chery’s Fulwin T11, already available in China. Measuring 5,205mm long, it is 385mm longer than the Jaecoo 8, with six seats arranged in a 2+2+2 configuration. Its range-extender hybrid system uses electric motors alongside a 1.5-litre petrol engine that generates electricity.

A Jaecoo 9 would take the brand beyond the affordable premium SUVs that established its reputation, potentially challenging considerably more expensive machinery. However, its final British specification, pricing and arrival date remain unconfirmed.

For TNY Design Studio, we’ve explored how the imposing Fulwin T11 could be transformed into a Jaecoo flagship, retaining its luxurious proportions while introducing the brand’s familiar styling.


Pricing could become one of the Jaecoo 9’s biggest advantages. With the smaller Jaecoo 8 starting at £45,500, TNY estimates the 9 could cost approximately £55,000–£60,000 in Britain. That would comfortably undercut the fully electric Kia EV9, priced from around £66,000, and Volvo EX90, starting at £73,160.

Reports suggest the Jaecoo 9 is destined for Britain, although the manufacturer has yet to announce a confirmed European launch date, specification or price. Much will depend on whether Chery’s range-extender hybrid technology can be adapted for European regulations. If Jaecoo gets the pricing right, its largest SUV could attract considerable attention.


While the Jaecoo 9 could take the brand further into luxury territory, an equally important opportunity lies at the opposite end of the market. In April 2026, Chery’s head of engineering, Peter Matkin, revealed that the company had begun developing a new platform for vehicles measuring less than four metres long. The aim is to compete in a substantial part of the European market that Chery’s predominantly SUV-focused range has yet to reach.

Although the project is underway, no launch date, specifications or intended brands have been confirmed. There is currently no official Jaecoo 2, but the new platform raises an interesting possibility.

For TNY Design Studio, we’ve imagined a compact Jaecoo hatchback measuring approximately 3.9 metres, bringing the brand’s distinctive styling into Fiat Grande Panda and Renault 5 territory.

Together, a potential Jaecoo 2 and Jaecoo 9 would represent two very different ambitions: affordable urban motoring at one end and six-seat luxury at the other. Between them, the 3, 5, 7 and 8 could form a remarkably comprehensive SUV-led range.

Jaecoo's arrival in Britain has been remarkably successful, but maintaining that momentum will require more than repeating the formula that made the 7 a bestseller. The forthcoming 3 could introduce the brand to a wider audience, while the 9 would test its appeal among luxury SUV buyers. Further ahead, Chery's smaller vehicle platform could open an entirely new chapter.

Not every possibility explored here will necessarily reach production, but together they illustrate just how much room Jaecoo has to grow. The real challenge will be turning that ambition into cars that British buyers genuinely want.

entry.title: An Estate for Every Budget – 12 of the Best from £2,000 to £20,000
entry.summary: Estate cars have long been among the most sensible vehicles on the road, but today's used market offers some particularly extraordinary value. From dependable family transport costing little more than £2,000 to enormous executive estates with almost 700 litres of luggage space, there's something here for virtually every budget. Spend a little…
entry.content:
Dacia Logan MCV Stepway

The Dacia Logan MCV earns its place here for one simple reason: extraordinary practicality for very little money. Its remarkable 573-litre boot beneath the parcel shelf expands to 1,518 litres with the rear seats folded. The load area is broad, square and refreshingly uncomplicated, making the Logan a compelling alternative to considerably more expensive family cars.

We've chosen the Stepway, although the cheapest Logan MCVs are conventional versions. The Stepway raises ground clearance by 50mm, while black wheelarch cladding, roof rails and more substantial bumpers give Dacia's deliberately simple design a surprisingly handsome, rugged appearance. It remains front-wheel-drive only, but that extra clearance is welcome on rough tracks and poorly maintained roads.

Higher-mileage Stepways can be found for less than £3,000, while a £5,000 budget opens up a wider selection of 0.9-litre turbocharged petrol and 1.5-litre diesel examples. Cars around 60,000 miles are worth hunting for, with both diesel and petrol models falling around the £5,000 mark.

For regularly carrying heavy loads, we'd favour the diesel. Its 220Nm of torque comfortably exceeds the petrol's 140Nm, and excellent fuel efficiency can help offset today's higher diesel prices, particularly over longer distances. The interior is basic and refinement modest, but few cars offer quite so much usable space for the money.


Škoda Fabia Estate

The Fabia Estate is arguably the best-value way into Škoda's famously practical estate-car range. It keeps everything refreshingly simple: a compact body, an uncomplicated interior and a genuinely impressive amount of luggage space. At just 4.26 metres long, it is easy to park and manoeuvre, yet offers a substantial 530-litre boot beneath the parcel shelf. Fold the rear seats and that expands to 1,395 litres.

Our preference is the 1.2 TSI petrol, particularly the 90PS and 110PS versions, which combine respectable performance with economical running costs. The four-cylinder engine also feels smoother and more relaxed than the later three-cylinder 1.0 TSI, particularly when the car is carrying passengers and luggage. Real-world economy around 48mpg is achievable, making the 1.2 a particularly appealing all-rounder.

Our £5,000 ceiling can secure a 2016–2017 example, with mileages generally starting around 90,000 at this price. The Fabia lacks the sheer carrying capacity of the Dacia Logan MCV, but compensates with a more polished driving experience, better-finished interior and compact dimensions.

For buyers who want a proper estate without the size or running costs of a larger car, the Fabia makes a remarkably convincing argument.


Fiat Tipo Station Wagon

The Fiat Tipo was something of a value champion when new, offering proper family-car space for considerably less money than its rivals. The Station Wagon originally started at just £13,995, and depreciation has only strengthened its appeal. Today, a £5,000 budget can stretch to a 2020 example, making the Tipo one of the newest estates at this price.

Practicality is its greatest strength. The generous 550-litre boot beneath the luggage cover is among the largest in its class, expanding to 1,650 litres with the rear seats folded. This creates a flat loading area capable of accommodating items up to 1.8 metres long. Passenger space is generous too, all wrapped up in an attractive, understated design that has aged rather well.

The 1.4 T-Jet turbocharged petrol offers lively performance, but real-world economy of around 40mpg is comfortably beaten by the 1.6-litre MultiJet diesel, which returns around 55mpg. With a substantial 320Nm of torque, it has the pulling power for heavy luggage, family holidays and towing, with a braked towing limit of up to 1,300kg on suitable versions.

Value becomes even more remarkable with earlier cars. 2017 Diesel estates covering around 100,000 miles can be found from £2,500, often with generous equipment levels. At these prices, the Tipo sets an exceptionally high benchmark for usable space per pound spent. For buyers covering longer distances, this could be one of the smartest purchases in the entire article.




Ford Mondeo Estate

The Ford Mondeo Estate is one of the great bargains of the used family car market. Large, comfortable and remarkably affordable, it delivers the sort of space and long-distance refinement that once made it a favourite with company drivers. Its generous cabin, supportive seats and composed motorway manners make it an excellent choice for families and anyone regularly covering longer journeys.

Practicality is equally impressive. The broad, accessible boot offers up to 525 litres beneath the luggage cover, expanding to 1,630 litres with the rear seats folded. There's plenty of room for passengers, while the long, usable loading area makes the Mondeo particularly well suited to bulky luggage and larger loads.

The 2.0 TDCi diesel is our preferred engine, with 150PS and 180PS versions delivering effortless motorway performance and real-world economy approaching 50mpg. Drivers covering shorter distances may find the 1.5 EcoBoost petrol a better fit. One important consideration is the later 2.0 EcoBlue diesel, introduced in 2019. This uses a wet timing-belt system, making correct oil specifications, documented servicing and adherence to Ford's replacement schedule important.

Our money would go on a well-equipped 2016–2017 2.0 TDCi. With £5,000–£8,000 securing attractive examples with fewer than 100,000 miles, the Mondeo offers an enormous amount of comfortable, practical motoring for the money.


Mercedes-Benz E-Class Estate

Few estate cars take load-lugging quite as seriously as the Mercedes-Benz E-Class. This generation was designed with practicality firmly in mind, combining enormous carrying capacity with the comfort, refinement and understated luxury expected of a Mercedes. Its sheer usefulness rivals that of many SUVs and MPVs, while remaining a particularly relaxing car for covering long motorway distances.

The boot is the real headline. In E250 CDI form, it offers a remarkable 695 litres beneath the luggage cover, some 135 litres more than the contemporary BMW 5 Series Touring. Fold the rear seats and capacity expands to 1,950 litres, extending that advantage to 280 litres. A wide opening, long load floor and self-levelling rear suspension further strengthen its credentials as a serious working estate.

The powerful 2.1-litre turbodiesel is an excellent match for the car, particularly the 204PS E250 CDI, which delivers 500Nm of torque. Unusually, Mercedes also offered the E300 BlueTEC Hybrid, combining a 2.1-litre diesel with electric assistance. It's an interesting alternative for economy-minded buyers, although boot capacity falls slightly to 650 litres.

£7,000–£10,000 secures attractive 2014–2015 examples with around 80,000–90,000 miles. We'd prioritise a comprehensive service history and excellent mechanical condition over optional extras. For buyers requiring carrying capacity without sacrificing comfort or a premium interior, this E-Class remains a compelling used purchase.


Peugeot 308 SW

The Peugeot 308 SW is one of the most convincing arguments for choosing an estate over an SUV. Its smart, understated exterior conceals exceptional practicality, while its manageable dimensions make it easy to live with. The 308 SW has also proved popular with British police forces, demonstrating its versatility as a working vehicle as well as a family car.

Practicality is a particular strength with 660 litres of boot space beneath the luggage cover, expanding to an impressive 1,775 litres with the rear seats folded. The low loading sill and flat-folding seats make excellent use of that space. Inside, the minimalist dashboard and large 9.7-inch touchscreen were remarkably forward-thinking for their time. Higher-specification GT models add sporty detailing, generous equipment and the option of a panoramic glass roof.

Our pick is the 2.0 BlueHDi GT automatic. Producing 180PS and 400Nm of torque, it combines strong performance with a smooth six-speed automatic gearbox, making it well suited to motorway journeys and heavier loads. Buyers prioritising fuel economy should consider the 1.6 BlueHDi, capable of around 60mpg in real-world conditions. The 1.2-litre turbo petrol is less convincing for frequent heavy loads or towing, and its wet timing belt requires attention to maintenance.

Remarkably, £6,000–£8,000 can secure a 2016–2017 2.0 BlueHDi GT automatic with approximately 50,000–80,000 miles. Considering its generous equipment, powerful drivetrain and enormous boot, the 308 SW represents outstanding value for buyers wanting something practical without sacrificing style or driving enjoyment.




Škoda Superb Estate

The Škoda Superb Estate has long been one of the most sensible large family cars on the market, combining executive-car comfort with exceptional practicality. What makes it particularly appealing today is the value. A new Superb Estate starts north of £38,000, yet our budget opens the door to the previous generation at a fraction of that price. It remains an impressive car, with generous equipment, strong build quality and a remarkably spacious interior.

The boot is among the largest in our entire selection, offering 660 litres beneath the luggage cover and an enormous 1,950 litres with the rear seats folded. The long, wide loading area makes transporting bulky items straightforward, while rear passengers enjoy exceptional legroom. 

The 2.0 TDI is our preferred engine, with the 150PS version offering an excellent balance of performance and economy. The more powerful 190PS diesel provides additional muscle for heavier loads and towing, while both suit the Superb's relaxed motorway character. TSI petrol engines can be perfectly pleasant for lighter duties, but fuel consumption is less appealing, especially when regularly carrying substantial loads.

Around £12,500 can secure a 2018 example with approximately 70,000–80,000 miles, although specification and service history influence prices considerably. We'd favour a well-maintained 2.0 TDI, checking the servicing record carefully, particularly on DSG automatics. For buyers wanting maximum space, comfort and long-distance ability without paying luxury-car money, the Superb is difficult to overlook.


Volkswagen Golf Estate

The Volkswagen Golf Estate offers an appealing middle ground between compact family cars and much larger load-luggers. At around 4.63 metres long, it's approximately 23cm shorter than the previous-generation Škoda Superb Estate, yet sacrifices surprisingly little luggage capacity.

The boot offers 611 litres with the rear seats upright, just 49 litres less than the Superb, expanding to an impressive 1,642 litres with them folded. A wide opening, adjustable boot floor and practical interior make excellent use of the available space. The eighth-generation Golf also brings a modern digital dashboard, generous safety equipment and a larger touchscreen than many similarly priced used estates.

Our preferred engine is the 2.0 TDI, available with 115PS or 150PS. It follows the same proven diesel formula as the larger Superb, delivering strong efficiency and relaxed motorway performance. The 150PS version is particularly appealing for regular heavy loads, although the 115PS diesel remains a sensible choice. The smaller 1.0 TSI petrol is adequate for lighter duties but feels less convincing when the estate is fully laden or towing.

A £12,000–£14,000 budget can secure a 2022 diesel estate with approximately 60,000–70,000 miles, while 2023 examples are worth watching at the upper end of that range. We'd prioritise service history and condition over trim level. For buyers wanting a relatively recent, economical estate with substantial carrying capacity but manageable exterior dimensions, the Golf makes an excellent case for itself.


Toyota Corolla Touring Sports

The Toyota Corolla Touring Sports brings something rather different to the estate car market: the space and practicality of a traditional family estate, combined with the remarkable efficiency of Toyota's self-charging hybrid system. The 1.8-litre petrol hybrid is our choice, delivering smooth automatic driving and excellent fuel economy without the need to plug in. Updated 2023 models also benefit from an increase in power to 140bhp.

Practicality remains impressive, with a generous 596-litre boot beneath the luggage cover, expanding to 1,606 litres with the rear seats folded. The loading area is wide and conveniently shaped, making the Corolla particularly useful for families and regular luggage carrying. Toyota even offers a two-seat Corolla Commercial van.

Efficiency is arguably the Corolla's greatest selling point, with around 60mpg achievable in everyday driving. Toyota's hybrid technology also has a reputation for longevity, with some Toyota hybrids exceeding 400,000 miles. While that is no guarantee for every example, a well-maintained Corolla makes a compelling long-term ownership proposition.

Our £13,000–£15,000 budget can secure a relatively recent 1.8 hybrid, with 2021–2022 examples offering plenty of choice with even 2023 examples appearing within this price bracket. With excellent economy, generous space and a proven hybrid pedigree, the Corolla is an estate designed to make financial sense for years to come.




Volvo V90

Few manufacturers have a stronger tradition of building estate cars than Volvo. From the famously practical estates of the past to the elegant V90, the Swedish manufacturer has long understood the appeal of combining generous space with comfort and understated luxury. Another familiar sight in British police fleets, the V90 is a particularly accomplished long-distance cruiser, with exceptionally comfortable seats, excellent refinement and a beautifully finished interior.

The V90 offers 560 litres of luggage space beneath the cover, expanding to 1,526 litres with the rear seats folded. Although its sleek roofline gives it a more elegant appearance than traditional Volvos, the loading area remains long, wide and genuinely useful. With almost two metres of load length available when the rear seats are folded, it is well suited to family holidays, bulky items and regular motorway journeys.

The 2.0-litre B4 petrol mild-hybrid produces 197bhp and offers a pleasing balance of performance and refinement, with around 37mpg achievable in everyday driving. Diesel versions offer better efficiency, potentially returning 50mpg, although they are relatively rare on the used market. Volvo ended diesel production in March 2024, bringing an end to an engine option particularly well suited to the V90's long-distance cruising abilities.

Around £18,000–£20,000 brings 2022 examples into consideration, including cars with approximately 50,000–60,000 miles. For those who value comfort, quality and effortless motorway performance, the V90 remains a wonderfully convincing alternative to buying an SUV.


BYD Seal 6 DM-i Touring 

The BYD Seal 6 DM-i Touring is perhaps the biggest surprise in our entire selection. Launched in Britain in late 2025, this is a genuinely modern plug-in hybrid estate, packed with technology and offering remarkable value. Buyers can secure an almost-new family car for considerably less than its original £34,990 asking price.

Practicality is impressive, with 500 litres of boot space beneath the luggage cover, expanding to 1,535 litres with the rear seats folded. There's generous passenger space too, while even the entry-level Boost includes a 12.8-inch touchscreen, reversing camera and powered tailgate.

The 1.5-litre plug-in hybrid combines petrol and electric power for smooth, economical driving. Boost models offer up to 31 miles of electric range, while the larger-battery Comfort stretches that to 62 miles. The petrol engine also makes longer journeys straightforward.

Our £20,000 budget can already secure a 2025 Boost with around 10,000 miles. Given its age, equipment and practicality, the Seal 6 represents extraordinary value, although its long-term reliability and resale performance remain largely unproven.


Vauxhall Astra Sports Tourer

The Volvo V90 and Škoda Superb demonstrate how easily estate cars can lose £20,000 through depreciation. The Vauxhall Astra Sports Tourer offers a clever alternative: buy one pre-registered for less than £20,000 and let the initial discount work in your favour. It's the only genuinely as-new estate available at this price.

The 130bhp 1.2-litre turbo petrol is our choice, with 2026 pre-registered examples advertised from just £18,995. Alternatively, £18,000–£20,000 can secure an all-electric 2025 model with around 5,000–10,000 miles. These can cover 256 miles of WLTP range, which is boosted to 275 miles in the newer version. Mild-hybrid and plug-in hybrid versions are also available, although they generally cost more when nearly new.

Despite its sleek styling, the Astra offers an impressive 597-litre boot, expanding to 1,634 litres with the rear seats folded. The electric version sacrifices some capacity to accommodate its battery, reducing those figures to 516 and 1,553 litres respectively.

Buyers seeking maximum practicality should also consider the closely related Peugeot 308 SW, which offers a slightly larger 608-litre boot and a more upmarket interior. However, the Peugeot generally costs more, meaning buyers may need to accept an older 2022–2025 example or higher mileage to remain within budget.



While traditional estates remain excellent all-rounders, buyers looking to maximise practicality should consider a few alternatives. These three models combine affordable running costs with clever, space-efficient designs, offering remarkable carrying capacity without the bulk or expense of a large SUV.


Citroën ë-Berlingo

Few vehicles demonstrate space-efficient design quite like the Citroën ë-Berlingo. Its upright, van-derived body maximises interior room without requiring the footprint of a large SUV. It's also a welcome example of British manufacturing, with electric Berlingos produced at Stellantis's Ellesmere Port factory in Cheshire.

The standard M version measures just 4.41 metres long yet offers an extraordinary 775-litre boot, expanding to 3,500 litres with the rear seats folded. The longer 4.76-metre XL can accommodate seven passengers, or provide 1,050 litres of luggage space in five-seat configuration. Fold the seats away and capacity stretches to an extraordinary 4,000 litres — more than twice that of the enormous Mercedes-Benz E-Class Estate.

The updated 52kWh battery gives the ë-Berlingo up to 213 miles of WLTP range, while its 136bhp motor provides smooth, effortless electric driving. Rapid charging at up to 100kW allows a 0–80% recharge in approximately 30 minutes. Range remains modest compared with larger electric cars, but affordable home charging makes everyday running costs particularly attractive.

The ë-Berlingo also offers impressive value when bought nearly new. Pre-registered examples are now available for less than £22,000, while low-mileage 2025 models are appearing from around £18,000, comfortably within our budget. For buyers prioritising maximum interior space, low running costs and modern electric motoring, few vehicles offer quite such a compelling package for the money.


Dacia Jogger Hybrid

The Dacia Jogger is one of the most versatile family cars available for the money. Combining the proportions of an estate with the flexibility of an MPV, it offers seven proper seats within a body measuring just 4.55 metres long. Its straightforward design prioritises usable space over expensive styling and unnecessary complexity.

With all seven seats occupied, boot capacity is a modest 160 litres. Fold the third row away and this increases to 565 litres, or 696 litres with those seats removed entirely. Maximum capacity reaches an impressive 1,807 litres with the second row folded, making the Jogger remarkably adaptable for family life.

Our choice is the 1.6-litre Hybrid 140. Its 140bhp output and automatic gearbox make easier work of carrying passengers and heavy luggage, while electric assistance helps reduce fuel consumption. Official economy reaches 56.5mpg, promising considerably lower fuel bills than many similarly spacious petrol-powered alternatives.

Around £16,000 can secure a 2023 Hybrid with approximately 30,000 miles, while £19,000 opens the door to a high-specification 2024 Extreme with around 10,000 miles. With seven-seat practicality, impressive efficiency and relatively modest running costs, the Jogger represents an enormous amount of family transport for the money.


Ford E-Tourneo Courier

The Ford E-Tourneo Courier proves that maximising interior space doesn't have to mean driving something enormous. At just 4.34 metres long, its upright proportions make excellent use of a compact footprint, while the angular styling and SUV-inspired front end give it a surprisingly sharp appearance for a van-derived family car.

Practicality is exceptional for its size. The five-seat Courier offers a generous 570-litre boot beneath the luggage cover, expanding to an impressive 2,162 litres with the rear seats folded and the space loaded to the roof. There's even an additional 44-litre compartment beneath the bonnet for charging cables and smaller items.

The earlier 43kWh electric model produces 136PS and offers up to 177 miles of WLTP range, making it particularly well suited to shorter journeys. The newer 46kWh version stretches that figure to 198 miles, although buyers wanting the additional range may need to increase their budget towards £23,000.

Early E-Tourneo Courier examples are now appearing below £20,000, making this an increasingly attractive alternative to a conventional estate. New examples also qualify for the full £3,750 UK Government Electric Car Grant, helping the Ford deliver strong value from new as well as used. For buyers prioritising space without unnecessary exterior bulk, it's a particularly clever package.

— What stands out most is just how much practicality the used market offers at every price point. From £2,500 diesels with enormous boots to nearly new plug-in hybrids and even pre-registered estates for less than £20,000, buyers have more choice than they might expect. And with some models offering close to 700 litres of luggage space, there's little reason to assume an SUV is the most practical option.

Whether your priority is fuel economy, long-distance comfort, seven seats or maximum carrying capacity, there's remarkable value to be found. The traditional estate remains one of motoring's most sensible ideas, and today's prices make the argument stronger than ever.

entry.title: Riversimple: What Comes After the Rasa? TNY Design Studio Explores
entry.summary: Hidden among the hills of Mid-Wales is a carmaker that has spent more than two decades questioning almost everything about the conventional car. Riversimple isn't chasing enormous batteries, huge horsepower figures or ever-heavier SUVs. Instead, founder Hugo Spowers and his team have pursued an unusually simple idea: build a genuinely lightweight hydrogen-electric…
entry.content:
For many, the first encounter with Riversimple came in early 2016, when the remarkable Rasa Alpha was unveiled. This was no conventional small car with its petrol engine replaced by a fuel cell. The two-seater had been engineered around efficiency from the outset, with a lightweight composite structure, four in-wheel electric motors and supercapacitors to capture braking energy and support acceleration.

The Alpha used an 8kW hydrogen fuel cell to sustain cruising and replenish stored energy. Riversimple quoted 0–60mph in a little over nine seconds, while the Rasa aimed for a range of roughly 300 miles on just 1.5kg of hydrogen and refuelling measured in minutes rather than hours. These were company targets rather than certified production-car figures.

The next important step was the Rasa Beta, unveiled in 2019 ahead of public trials beginning in 2020. It featured a larger 12kW fuel cell and further refinements to packaging, software and energy management. Trial vehicles gathered valuable experience through projects in Abergavenny and Pembrokeshire, helping transform the Rasa from an experimental concept into a working test bed for Riversimple's wider ambitions.


That brings us to our first Design Studio rendering: a compact, more conventional two-seat Riversimple hatchback. We've retained the brand's flowing surfaces but imagined an everyday shape with a more useful rear end. The result is less experimental than the Rasa. It asks a simple question: if Riversimple wants to bring hydrogen motoring to ordinary drivers, could a small, efficient runabout be the right starting point?

It's not a model invented entirely from thin air. Riversimple's own waiting-list page outlines a proposed two-door, two-seat hatchback with a minimum 330-mile range, a targeted 0–60mph time of 9.5 seconds and a three-minute refuelling time. The company says its proposed subscription and mileage charges are intended to deliver total running costs comparable with a basic petrol MINI. That is a target for the complete cost of motoring, not an announced vehicle purchase price.

Our illustration is an independent TNY interpretation rather than an official Riversimple design. Seen alongside the Morgan LIFECar, Hyrban and two generations of Rasa, it would represent another step in a long line of experimental two-seat concepts. But bringing such a car into production would require more than attractive styling: funding, reliable hydrogen supply, customer support and the capacity to build vehicles consistently all remain crucial.


Riversimple's planned business model is almost as unusual as its cars. Rather than selling the vehicle to the customer, the company intends to retain ownership and charge a fixed monthly subscription plus a mileage rate.

Its proposed package includes insurance, maintenance, tyres and even hydrogen fuel. The driver pays to use the car rather than to buy it outright. Riversimple explains its proposed subscription service on its website.

To understand the Rasa, it's worth travelling back to 2009. The Riversimple Hyrban was a compact, two-seat technology demonstrator developed over the following years to test the company's network-electric approach. Its 6kW powertrain combined a hydrogen fuel cell with supercapacitors, using stored braking energy for bursts of acceleration while the fuel cell handled more constant demands.

Riversimple quoted 0–50mph in around eight seconds and a 50mph cruising capability. They aren't dazzling performance figures by modern standards, but for such a tiny fuel-cell system they represented an important achievement.

The Hyrban demonstrated that remarkable efficiency did not necessarily have to mean an impractically slow car. One example became part of the Science Museum's collection — a fitting recognition of an unusual piece of British engineering.


Riversimple's history also includes one of Britain's most traditional sports-car names. Between 2005 and 2008, Hugo Spowers and collaborators including the Morgan Motor Company worked on the extraordinary Morgan LIFECar — a research project designed to explore how hydrogen-electric technology could meet the expectations of a lightweight sports car.

Revealed at the 2008 Geneva Motor Show, the LIFECar brought together Morgan's distinctive approach to car design with advanced fuel-cell research. It was a development demonstrator, not a showroom model, but it helped show that hydrogen propulsion could be interesting for reasons other than economy alone. Behind that striking bodywork lay the early thinking that would eventually feed into the much smaller Hyrban and Rasa.

Hugo Spowers had established OScar Automotive in the early 2000s after a career in motorsport; the business became Riversimple in 2007. By 2026, the venture's roots therefore stretched back roughly a quarter of a century. It's a remarkably long period of continuous experimentation for a small independent automotive project, and one that makes the company's persistence especially noteworthy.


Our second new rendering asks what happens when Riversimple goes beyond two seats. Until now, its best-known experimental cars have favoured small passenger compartments and very low weight. That's helped efficiency, packaging and aerodynamics, but it also restricts the number of people who can use them. A genuinely practical four-seater could introduce Riversimple to a far wider audience.

Again, there is real substance behind the speculation. Riversimple's own proposed range includes a two-door, four-seat hatchback with a minimum 300-mile range and a targeted 0–60mph time of 10.5 seconds. The company indicates that its subscription and mileage charges would be about 5% higher than for the two-seater. If achievable, that's an intriguing trade-off for two extra seats.

And there's an encouraging new development. In 2026, Riversimple announced its leadership of the £1.7 million ZELLOR project, aiming to demonstrate a four-seat hydrogen-electric vehicle weighing less than 1,000kg and capable of more than 400 miles. 

Meanwhile, hydrogen passenger cars have not disappeared from the international picture. Toyota continues developing the Mirai, Hyundai has introduced a new-generation NEXO, and BMW is preparing a hydrogen-powered version of its next X5 for series production in 2028 using fuel-cell technology developed with Toyota.

These are much larger and heavier vehicles than Riversimple's designs, but they underline that fuel-cell development continues across the industry. Perhaps a tiny Welsh manufacturer could find its own place in that market.


The third TNY design is a compact, two-seat commercial van. We've retained the passenger car's front end and overall height while extending and squaring off the rear bodywork to create a more useful load space. A small van doesn't need sports-car acceleration or luxury equipment; for urban deliveries and local services, ease of use, running costs and availability often matter more.

Riversimple is already considering this category. Its official waiting list includes a small runabout van with the same projected range, performance and subscription pricing as the two-seat hatchback. Shared engineering could therefore become an important part of a future vehicle family, although Riversimple has not confirmed final production specifications, dimensions or payload capacities.

Hydrogen also has a foothold in British commercial transport. Northern Ireland manufacturer Wrightbus builds fuel-cell buses including the StreetDeck Hydroliner, with examples used in UK public transport.

Larger fleet operators can sometimes support dedicated refuelling facilities and predictable routes, something private motorists rarely can. A lightweight Riversimple van could suit that localised model, especially where other hydrogen vehicles already operate.

However, a bus depot's hydrogen pump is not automatically a public filling station, and hydrogen supply remains a major challenge. Fleet growth might help justify new infrastructure, but will not necessarily create a convenient national network for car drivers. That's why a regional deployment strategy may be a more realistic first step than an immediate nationwide launch.


And yet the Riversimple story reaches further back than the LIFECar. In 2004, Hugo Spowers was involved in the tiny, single-seat BOC Shell Eco-Marathon project, developed with BOC, siGEN, Shetland Composites and OScar Automotive. Looking at the little blue-and-white machine today, it seems almost impossibly distant from the more polished Rasas.

The figures remain remarkable: a vehicle weighing approximately 40kg, powered by a 25-watt hydrogen fuel cell, and engineered around a target efficiency exceeding 10,795mpg equivalent.

Riversimple has described a theoretical ability to travel around the world using the energy equivalent of just two gallons of fuel. That was a comparison illustrating its extraordinary efficiency ambitions, not a claim that the vehicle was a practical road car capable of such a journey.

It was an experiment, but an important one. The recurring Riversimple principles — minimise weight, reduce energy demand and rethink familiar automotive assumptions — were already visible more than twenty years ago.


For a company that has not yet become a mass-market carmaker, Riversimple has a surprisingly substantial history. It has created several generations of working hydrogen vehicles, developed an unusual low-power architecture, put Rasas into real-world trials and kept specialist engineering activity in Wales. 

There are also practical challenges to overcome. Battery-electric cars have moved into the mainstream, while hydrogen passenger vehicles remain a niche market. Producing, transporting and dispensing hydrogen all involve costs and energy use, while its environmental benefits depend on how the fuel is made.

Public hydrogen filling stations remain scarce across Britain. Refuelling in just three minutes is an attractive prospect, but a much wider infrastructure network will be needed to unlock the technology's full potential.

But it would be a mistake to confuse those obstacles with a lack of progress. Hydrogen is finding applications in some buses and other fleet vehicles, and manufacturers such as Toyota, Hyundai and BMW continue investing in fuel-cell technology.

Riversimple's particularly lightweight approach offers another possibility entirely: use much less hydrogen in the first place. With the ZELLOR project underway and three possible vehicle types outlined, there are still genuinely interesting chapters to be written.


From a 40kg economy experiment in 2004 to the Rasa, public trials and today's ambitions for more practical vehicles, Riversimple has followed a path very different from the rest of the industry. Our two-seat hatchback, four-seater and compact van are TNY Design Studio's interpretations of where that journey might lead, not previews of confirmed production models.

Yet the company itself is considering all three categories, and its latest engineering programme provides a reason to keep paying attention. Electric cars may dominate the headlines, but there could still be room for a small Welsh company prepared to approach hydrogen from an entirely different angle.

The real challenge now is turning decades of intriguing engineering into everyday vehicles that people can actually use.

entry.title: Taking on the X5 – Mercedes' Next Generation of Luxury SUVs
entry.summary: Mercedes-Benz helped shape the premium SUV market long before BMW joined the party. The original M-Class arrived in 1997, two years ahead of the first BMW X5, at a time when the Range Rover was still the established benchmark for luxury off-roaders. Originally known as the M-Class or ML, the model became…
entry.content:
Mercedes certainly hasn't been standing still. Unveiled on 17 October 2026, the new all-electric Mercedes-AMG GT SUV delivers up to an extraordinary 1,153bhp, with a maximum WLTP range of around 435 miles and charging speeds of up to 710kW. It's a formidable new arrival that could challenge the performance end of BMW's electric SUV range.

However, BMW's fifth-generation X5 takes a broader approach, offering petrol, diesel, plug-in hybrid and fully electric powertrains, with a hydrogen fuel-cell version planned for 2028.

That leaves Mercedes needing more than an electric performance flagship to answer BMW's challenge. So, what should the next-generation GLE look like? TNY Design Studio explores three possibilities, starting with the conventional GLE SUV.


Across four generations, the M-Class and later GLE have become one of Mercedes-Benz's most important SUVs, with TNY estimating approximately 3.5 million sold worldwide since 1997. A fifth generation therefore has a difficult job: modernising an established favourite without losing its identity.

For our proposed 2028 GLE, TNY Design Studio has made one particularly significant departure. We've abandoned the distinctive rear quarter-window and C-pillar treatment that has been a defining feature of the M-Class since 1997, replacing it with a cleaner, more conventional glasshouse inspired by the latest GLC.

Combined with a more imposing front end, sharper detailing and a cleaner body design, our interpretation aims to bring the GLE into Mercedes' next design era. With BMW moving its new X5 closer to five metres in length, Mercedes has an opportunity to make its fifth-generation GLE feel like a genuine step forward, rather than another evolution of the familiar formula.


Since its introduction in 2015, the GLE Coupé has established itself as an important part of Mercedes-Benz's SUV family, offering a sportier alternative to the conventional GLE and a direct rival to BMW's X6.

However, Mercedes' more recent SUV designs haven't all enjoyed the same reception. The all-electric EQE SUV has struggled to establish itself in some markets, with its rounded, aerodynamically focused styling dividing opinion. The newly revealed Mercedes-AMG GT SUV suggests a change of direction, embracing a more striking, muscular and dynamic appearance.

For our proposed 2028 GLE Coupé, TNY Design Studio takes a slightly different approach. Rather than exaggerating the sloping roofline, we've introduced a more elegant, saloon-inspired rear profile, creating something between a traditional SUV Coupé and a raised luxury saloon.

The result is an interpretation that prioritises elegance over aggression, while retaining the road presence expected of a Mercedes-Benz luxury SUV.

Mercedes-Benz has never been afraid to experiment with its larger luxury vehicles. Introduced in 2005, the original R-Class combined elements of an estate car, MPV and SUV into something rather unusual. Offering six or seven seats, generous interior space and the comfort of a luxury saloon, it was intended to create an entirely new category of premium family transport.

Commercially, however, the R-Class never achieved the success Mercedes had hoped for. Sales disappointed in Europe and North America, although the model enjoyed a longer life in China.

Nevertheless, the R-Class demonstrated Mercedes' willingness to explore unconventional ideas within the potentially lucrative premium SUV market, rather than simply following established formulas.

Two decades later, with luxury SUVs more popular and diverse than ever, could Mercedes be tempted to experiment again?

If Mercedes-Benz was ever going to revisit the R-Class idea, now may be the time. When the original arrived, its blend of SUV, estate and MPV qualities felt unusual. Today, however, the market is far more open to experimental luxury vehicles, while premium MPVs have become a much more established part of the high-end family car market.

That creates an interesting opportunity for Mercedes. A modern successor could offer something genuinely different from the familiar large-SUV formula, combining the road presence buyers expect with greater cabin space, easier access and a more versatile interior.

Our proposed GLR keeps broadly similar dimensions to the original R-Class, preserving its long, substantial silhouette, but reinterprets the concept using Mercedes' modern design language. The result is less awkward and more cohesive, blending MPV practicality with the cleaner surfacing, sharper lighting and stronger front-end presence expected of a contemporary Mercedes-Benz.

Could this finally be the right time for Mercedes to try again?


BMW's latest X5 highlights the challenge facing Mercedes. What began as a straightforward rivalry between two large premium SUVs has developed into a much broader contest, encompassing SUV coupés, electric models and high-performance flagships.

With the fifth-generation X5 approaching five metres in length and offering an unusually broad range of powertrains, Mercedes needs to consider not only how its next GLE looks, but also where it fits within an increasingly competitive luxury SUV market.

So, how closely matched are the two manufacturers' existing line-ups?

Perhaps the biggest surprise is just how closely matched these models are. The outgoing BMW X5 is only 12mm longer than the current GLE, while the GLE Coupé and X6 are separated by just 20mm.

Although BMW's new X5 is growing, extra length alone won't define the next generation. Mercedes must find ways to make its luxury SUVs feel distinctive, rather than simply matching its rival's dimensions.

And as our final image illustrates, the next GLE could represent something more significant: a departure from almost three decades of familiar M-Class design.


For Mercedes-Benz, taking on the X5 shouldn't simply mean building a larger GLE. BMW's expanding range demonstrates how diverse the luxury SUV market has become, but Mercedes has the heritage and engineering expertise to respond in its own way.

Our proposed fifth-generation GLE brings a familiar favourite into a cleaner design era, while the GLE Coupé explores a more elegant alternative to the traditional SUV fastback. The GLR is perhaps the boldest proposal of all, reviving the versatility of the R-Class for a market that might finally appreciate it.

Whether Mercedes chooses evolution or something more adventurous, its next generation needs to offer more than just a new grille.

entry.title: The Next Microcar Generation – Six Little Cars with Big Ambitions
entry.summary: Microcars might occupy a small corner of Europe's automotive market, but their appeal is difficult to ignore. In 2025, France registered 24,919 new light quadricycles, while Italy recorded 17,989 light and heavy quadricycles, more than 72% of them electric. Their appeal lies in simplicity. Compact dimensions, low energy consumption and modest running…
entry.content:
Chinese manufacturer Bontu is bringing its electric microcars to Europe, having introduced the range in Milan earlier this year. Among the newcomers is the BT09, a compact, affordable alternative to established models such as the Citroën Ami.

Measuring just 2,750mm long and 1,450mm wide, the BT09 comes in two versions. The two-seat L6e model has a 7.68kWh battery, offering a claimed 81-mile range and a 28mph top speed. A more capable four-seat L7e version increases battery capacity to 10kWh, range to approximately 93 miles and top speed to 47mph.

Italian pricing is expected to start around €9,500, making it an interesting proposition for budget-conscious buyers.

Stepping up from the smaller BT09, the Bontu BTE05 offers considerably more space and performance, potentially making it a more convincing alternative to a conventional city car.

Measuring 3,000mm long, 1,500mm wide and 1,630mm tall, the BTE05 is available with two or four seats. Buyers can choose between 13.9kWh and 18.1kWh LFP batteries, delivering claimed ranges of 106 and 138 miles respectively. Its 56mph top speed also makes it considerably more versatile than a typical 28mph microcar.

Equipment is surprisingly generous, including air conditioning, ABS, a driver's airbag and a 12-inch touchscreen.

European pricing has been estimated at €14,000–€17,000 (approximately £12,000–£15,000), although official prices remain unconfirmed. Bontu is establishing itself in Italy, but a British launch has yet to be announced.

Perhaps the most significant newcomer is the Dacia Hipster, a remarkably simple electric microcar designed to bring affordable motoring to a wider audience.

Measuring just 3,000mm long, 1,550mm wide and 1,530mm tall, the boxy Hipster manages four proper seats and a 70-litre boot, expanding to 500 litres with the rear seats folded. Weighing under 800kg, the concept is approximately 20% lighter than the Dacia Spring.

Reports suggest production could begin in China during 2027, with a 15kWh battery, approximately 20bhp and a targeted UK price below £10,000.

That could make the Hipster one of Britain's most affordable new electric vehicles, although production and pricing remain unconfirmed by Dacia. Its combination of four seats, clever packaging and potentially accessible pricing could make it a particularly important addition to the emerging L7e market.

Fiat's growing microcar ambitions now extend well beyond the familiar Topolino. The Italian manufacturer has three distinct approaches to micromobility: the two-seat Topolino, the three-wheeled Tris commercial vehicle and the four-seat Multiplina.

First revealed in July 2026 and subsequently displayed at the Paris Motor Show, the Multiplina takes inspiration from the original 1956 Fiat 600 Multipla, promising considerably greater practicality than its smaller siblings.

While the Topolino measures just 2,558mm long, offers 46 miles of range and is limited to 28mph, the Multiplina aims to accommodate four occupants within a body measuring under three metres. Developed around the L7e heavy quadricycle category, it could offer a 56mph top speed, greater power and a larger battery.

Production has been suggested for 2028, although Fiat is still working to reduce weight to meet quadricycle regulations. Pricing, battery specifications and UK availability remain unconfirmed.

Chinese newcomer Linktour is moving quickly into Europe, with its Alumi electric microcar already available in several continental markets. Following its British Motor Show debut in August 2026, the manufacturer is preparing to introduce three versions to the UK.

Measuring just 2,685mm long and 1,500mm wide, the two-seat Alumi features lightweight aluminium construction, frameless doors and a surprisingly contemporary interior.

The L6e Alumi and Alumi Pro offer a 7.2kWh battery, up to 75 miles of claimed range and a 28mph top speed. The more powerful L7e Elite+ increases capacity to 12.96kWh, delivering up to 112 miles and 56mph.

Belgian prices start at €10,490 for the Alumi and €14,990 for the Elite, equivalent to approximately £8,850 and £12,650. British prices and dealer availability remain unconfirmed, but Linktour's UK arrival appears increasingly close.


Spanish newcomer LIUX is taking an unusual approach to electric microcars, with its BIG making an international debut at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. Its most distinctive feature is a lightweight flax-fibre composite monocoque supported by a steel chassis, combining structural strength with reduced weight and environmental impact.

Measuring approximately 2,700mm long and 1,500mm wide, the two-seat L7e quadricycle weighs just 648kg and offers a surprisingly useful 240-litre boot. Two LFP battery options, 15kWh and 20kWh, promise 134 and 168 miles respectively under WMTC testing. Power comes from a 47bhp electric motor, with a 56mph top speed.

Production is planned for Spain, with deliveries expected during the first half of 2027. Prices should start below €18,000 (approximately £15,200), with Spain, France and Italy the initial markets.

UK availability remains unconfirmed, but the BIG's lightweight construction and impressive claimed efficiency make it one of Europe's more intriguing microcar newcomers.


For decades, Europe's microcar market was largely the territory of specialist manufacturers such as Aixam, Ligier and Microcar. More recently, mainstream manufacturers have joined the conversation, with the Renault Twizy, Citroën Ami, Opel Rocks Electric and Fiat Topolino introducing a new generation of buyers to tiny electric vehicles.

Now the segment appears ready for another wave of newcomers. Established carmakers are exploring greater practicality and affordability, while ambitious new manufacturers are introducing fresh designs, lightweight construction and increasingly capable electric powertrains.

For Britain, the question remains whether these vehicles can move beyond niche appeal and establish themselves as genuinely useful alternatives to conventional cars.

Not all six newcomers will necessarily reach UK showrooms, but the growing variety suggests that Europe's smallest vehicles could have a much bigger future than their modest dimensions might suggest.

entry.title: Back to the Future – Reimagining the Mitsubishi i for Europe
entry.summary: Few small cars have been as quietly ambitious as the Mitsubishi i. Launched in Japan with a rear-mounted petrol engine, it later became the i-MiEV, one of the earliest mass-produced electric cars. Two decades on, Mitsubishi is again leaning heavily on partnerships, with Renault-derived models underpinning much of its European range. Yet…
entry.content:
The Mitsubishi i arrived in Japan in 2006 as a kei car, measuring just 3,395mm long and 1,475mm wide. Yet its rounded, almost futuristic body concealed some remarkably clever engineering.

By positioning a 659cc three-cylinder petrol engine ahead of the rear axle, Mitsubishi could push the wheels towards the corners, achieve a 2,550mm wheelbase and create surprisingly generous space for four occupants.

Rear-wheel drive, sophisticated De Dion rear suspension and a four-speed automatic made the i rather more interesting than the average city car. Britain even received the turbocharged petrol version in 2007, priced at around £9,000, although it remained a rare sight.

More importantly for Europe, its unconventional packaging provided the perfect foundation for the electric i-MiEV, which would later underpin the Peugeot iOn and Citroën C-Zero. (Image credit: Mitsubishi)

For our 2028 interpretation, TNY Design Studio imagines the Mitsubishi i returning on Renault's new Twingo E-Tech platform. At 3,790mm long and 1,720mm wide, it's noticeably larger than the original i-MiEV, but still compact. Our rendering retains the rounded cabin, distinctive proportions and playful character, updated with Mitsubishi's latest design language.

A Twingo-based i could inherit Renault's 27.5kWh LFP battery and 82PS motor, delivering up to 163 miles of WLTP range. That's a considerable improvement over the original i-MiEV's 16kWh battery, 67PS motor and 93-mile NEDC range, although the testing standards differ.

Practicality could improve too. Where the i-MiEV offered just 166 litres of boot space due partly to its rear-mounted powertrain, the Twingo provides up to 360 litres with its independently sliding rear seats pushed forward. A revived i could offer similar flexibility without sacrificing its city-friendly dimensions.



From the rear, our Mitsubishi i rendering retains one of the original car's most distinctive features: its high-mounted rear light clusters, now reimagined as slim vertical LED strips alongside the rear window. We've deliberately kept the tailgate and surrounding bodywork clean, preserving the simplicity that made the first-generation i so appealing.

There's also a logical place for it in Mitsubishi's European range. The Renault Clio-based Colt measures 4,053mm long, while the new electric Twingo is just 3,790mm, leaving a 263mm difference between the two.

A revived i could comfortably sit beneath the Colt, offering an affordable, four-seat electric city car without competing directly with its larger sibling. With Mitsubishi already relying on Renault for several European models, extending that relationship into the smallest segment seems an entirely plausible next step.


Renault's new Twingo is set to provide the foundations for a growing family of affordable electric city cars across the Renault-Nissan-Mitsubishi Alliance. The next-generation Dacia Spring and Nissan Pixo are both set to draw on the same architecture, with TNY having previously explored both models through our own Design Studio renderings.

Could Mitsubishi be the next brand to join this expanding family?

Our entry-level Mitsubishi i rendering imagines how an especially affordable version might look. Finished in non-metallic paint, with simple wheel trims, unpainted plastic mirrors and simplified lighting, it deliberately avoids unnecessary decoration.

For Mitsubishi, a revived i wouldn't need to be complicated or expensive. A straightforward, affordable electric city car could fill a noticeable gap in its European range, bringing back some of the originality and small-car ingenuity that made the first generation so interesting.


The original Mitsubishi i was a small car with big ideas, proving that clever engineering could make even the tiniest vehicles feel innovative. Its electric successor arrived ahead of its time, helping to lay the foundations for an industry-wide shift towards electrification.

Nearly two decades later, the market looks very different. Affordable electric city cars are finally beginning to gain momentum, and Mitsubishi already has access to the technology through its relationship with Renault.

A revived i wouldn't need to reinvent the electric car. It would simply need to be affordable, practical and distinctive, much like the original. For a brand rebuilding its European presence, perhaps looking back at one of its smallest creations could be a very sensible way forward.
